passage:
Nazia, you asked about my garden. I'm Madhav. For three years, I hand-built a watering system on our terrace: bamboo pipes, clay pots, a timer I soldered myself.
I loved it. But half the plants died every summer because the timer failed.
Last month I finally asked myself: if I were starting fresh today, would I build this, or buy a simple drip kit? Honestly? I'd buy the kit.
It was hard. I felt like I was throwing away three years. But I kept the bamboo pipes for the jasmine by the door, where they work fine, and I kept my soldered timer in a drawer.
This summer, nothing died. And I'm still proud of the bamboo.

qa.q: What did Madhav build on the terrace?
qa.a: Madhav hand-built a watering system on the terrace.

qa.q: What did Madhav feel when deciding to buy the drip kit?
qa.a: Madhav felt torn and sad, as if throwing away three years, but clear about the choice.

qa.q: How did Madhav honour the effort while choosing the better option?
qa.a: Madhav kept the bamboo pipes for the jasmine and saved the timer, while using the drip kit for the rest.

qa.q: How might Nazia see Madhav's decision?
qa.a: Nazia might see it as wise and a little brave, since Madhav chose what works without dismissing the work.

grounding: Shows an adult asking whether they'd choose their handmade system if starting fresh today, separating pride in the labour from the result.

passage:
I've watched Ishita build her own recipe app for two years, evenings and weekends. I'm Joseph, her flatmate.
Last month she got a job offer at a big food company. They wanted her to use their app platform for her recipes, and drop her own.
She was upset for days. "It's my work," she said. "Every screen is mine."
Then one evening I heard her ask herself out loud, "If I were starting today, would I build this, or use theirs?" She sat with it for a long time.
She said yes to the job. She moved her recipes to their platform. But she kept her own app running for her family, and she still smiles when she opens it.

qa.q: How long had Ishita built her recipe app?
qa.a: She built it for two years, evenings and weekends.

qa.q: How does Joseph seem to feel about Ishita's decision?
qa.a: Joseph seems respectful and a little moved, having watched how hard it was for her.

qa.q: What question helped Ishita decide, and why?
qa.a: "If I were starting today, would I build this?" It helped her separate pride in her work from what serves her best now.

qa.q: How does Ishita feel about her own app?
qa.a: She is proud and attached to it, and still smiles when she opens it, even after moving on.

grounding: Shows an observer watching a young adult ask whether she would choose her self-built app if starting fresh, while still cherishing it.

passage:
Diwali cleaning day
I was halfway through my 300-piece jungle puzzle on the floor when Mummy called me to help clean the fans. I'm Yamini.
All through the cleaning, I kept thinking about the tiger's missing ear. Shankar asked me to pass the duster twice and I didn't hear him. I finished the curtains, then the shelves, and I don't even remember doing them.
The moment Mummy said, "Done!" I ran back to the puzzle. I found the tiger's ear in five minutes.
Funny thing: I've finished lots of puzzles and can't remember any of them. But this one I couldn't stop thinking about, just because it wasn't done.

qa.q: How many pieces was Yamini's puzzle?
qa.a: It was a 300-piece jungle puzzle.

qa.q: Why didn't Yamini hear Shankar ask for the duster?
qa.a: Yamini felt restless and distracted, still thinking about the unfinished puzzle.

qa.q: What could help Yamini focus on cleaning next time?
qa.a: Yamini could stop the puzzle at a clear point, or note the next piece to find, so it doesn't keep nagging.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel when Yamini doesn't hear?
qa.a: Shankar may feel a bit annoyed, having to ask twice while Yamini's mind is elsewhere.

grounding: Shows a child called away mid-puzzle during festival cleaning who keeps thinking about it and rushes back, while finished tasks slip away.

It was the summer holidays in the village, and Aditi was halfway through a wooden animal puzzle her Nani had bought at the fair. The elephant was missing its trunk.
Then Sangeeta, her cousin, called from the lane: "Aditi! The mangoes are ready, come pick!"
Aditi went. But under the mango tree, she kept thinking about the trunk. Where had that piece gone? Was it under the charpai? She dropped two mangoes.
"Aditi, what's wrong with you today?" Sangeeta laughed.
"The trunk!"
Aditi ran home before the basket was full. She found the piece under the charpai. Once the elephant was done, she forgot about it and went back to the mangoes.

qa.q: What piece was missing from the elephant?
qa.a: The elephant was missing its trunk.

qa.q: Why did Aditi drop two mangoes?
qa.a: She was restless and distracted, thinking about the unfinished puzzle.

qa.q: What could Aditi do next time she has to leave a puzzle?
qa.a: She could note where she thinks the missing piece is, so her mind can let go until she returns.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta see Aditi running home?
qa.a: Sangeeta may be amused and puzzled, not knowing a missing trunk was nagging her cousin.

grounding: Shows a child called away from an unfinished puzzle who keeps thinking about it and rushes back, then forgets it once done.

passage:
It was the first night of Hanukkah in Haifa, and Noa was halfway through a jigsaw of the sea. Only the boat was left.
Her mother called, "Noa, candle time!" Noa went to the window with the family. She sang, but her eyes kept drifting to the table.
"Noa, where are you?" her cousin Olga whispered.
"The boat," Noa whispered back.
After the candles, everyone sat down to eat. Noa ate fast and slipped back to the puzzle. In ten minutes, the boat was done. She sighed happily.
The next day she couldn't remember what the finished puzzle looked like. But she remembered the boat that wasn't done.

qa.q: What part of the puzzle was left?
qa.a: Only the boat was left.

qa.q: What was Noa feeling as her eyes drifted to the table?
qa.a: She felt restless and pulled back to the unfinished puzzle.

qa.q: What could help Noa enjoy the candles without distraction next time?
qa.a: She could finish the puzzle earlier or tell herself exactly what's left, so it doesn't keep calling her.

qa.q: How might Olga feel when Noa whispers "The boat"?
qa.a: Olga may feel amused and a little puzzled by how much the puzzle holds Noa's mind.

grounding: Shows a child called away mid-puzzle during a festival who keeps thinking about it and rushes back to finish, while the finished puzzle soon slips from mind.

It was 12:40 at night in Amandeep's Chandigarh flat. The episode ended with the detective opening a door, a scream, and black screen. "Next episode in 5... 4..."
Amandeep had said "one more" three episodes ago. He had a chemistry test at nine.
He texted Mohit: "bro did u see ep 7. WHO SCREAMED"
Mohit replied: "not telling. watch it."
Amandeep put the phone down, turned off the light and lay there. The scream played in his head. What was behind the door?
At 12:55 he turned the light back on. "Just this one," he whispered.

qa.q: What time did Amandeep's chemistry test start?
qa.a: He had a chemistry test at nine.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep turn the light back on?
qa.a: He felt restless and couldn't stop wondering about the scream, so the unfinished story pulled him back.

qa.q: What could Amandeep try to stop watching at night?
qa.a: He could stop in the middle of an episode instead of at the cliffhanger, or write down his guess so his mind can rest.

qa.q: How might Mohit's reply affect Amandeep?
qa.a: Mohit's teasing reply makes Amandeep even more curious, strengthening the pull to keep watching.

grounding: Shows a teenager who can't stop thinking about a cliffhanger and watches one more episode late at night.

"Trisha, you look terrible."
"Kunal, I slept at three."
"Three? Why?"
"The show. Episode six ended with the sister getting into a stranger's car. How could I sleep?"
"So you watched seven?"

"Want to know a trick? Stop in the middle of an episode, not the end."

passage:
Last winter, I learned something about myself. I'm Nirmala. There was a series everyone at school was watching, and every episode ended on a cliffhanger.
One night, episode four ended with the main character falling off a roof. I had board exam prep the next morning. I told myself, "Tomorrow." But I couldn't stop thinking about it. Did he survive? I lay awake for an hour.
At one, I gave up and watched episode five. Then six.
My brother Vaibhav found me at breakfast, eyes red. "You look like you fell off a roof," he said.
Now I stop in the middle of an episode. When the story is still open but not screaming, I can actually sleep.

qa.q: What happened at the end of episode four?
qa.a: The main character fell off a roof.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling lying awake for an hour?
qa.a: Nirmala felt restless and couldn't stop wondering what happened, pulled back by the open story.

qa.q: What change did Nirmala make, and why does it help?
qa.a: Nirmala now stops in the middle of an episode, so no cliffhanger is left nagging at bedtime.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav have felt seeing Nirmala at breakfast?
qa.a: Vaibhav was probably amused, teasing about the red eyes, but maybe a little concerned too.

grounding: Shows a teenager unable to stop thinking about a cliffhanger and watching more episodes, then learning to stop mid-episode.
